It's complicated...

Computers nowadays use binary because it's simple, and you can represent every number in binary that you can wih trinary. However, a "trit" would contain more information than a "bit", and therefore you could pack more data in a similar number of units.

Then the question becomes, how do you encode those trits? Bits are simple; on/off, voltage/no voltage. You could use different voltage levels, 0V for a 0, 0.5V for a 1, and 1.0V for a 2...

Then you realize, if trinary logic gives you more data density, then higher bases would be even more dense! Hell, you could even do a decimal computer directly! Or use a base that's a multiple of 2 and you could still use binary logic for calculations.

All in all, though, binary is established and simple, and I doubt it'll be supplanted in general in the near future.

It will be supplanted when Moore's law expires due to physical constraints being reached. Then, the power of quantum physics will be exploited to keep the growth of computing power -- not hardware -- increasing in a similar exponential manner.
Except current quantum computing still uses binary bits. :-)

For the most part, they don't offer anything that can't already be done with binary computers anyway.

It adds a lot of complexity and a few more ways for the computer to go wrong, as well.

Edit - most math that's done in binary would take the same number of CPU cycles to do in trinary or any other base, so there's no real performance gain there. You'll also have to add an entirely new set of circuits to detect the difference between 1 and 2, as well as the difference between 0 and 1.
